title: Phaedra - National Theatre - Review with photos of a story of forbidden love
transcript: hello and welcome to theater reviews with all seven on the whole I loved fedra by Simon stone at the national theater's Littleton Auditorium there was rarely just one element I didn't like but first let me tell you what was so good about it don't worry if you're not keen on Greek tragedy this is not a production full of togas and choruses it's a bad up-to-date tale of a politician who has an affair the essential story of Federer is still there as told in ancient Greece by euripides in ancient Rome by Seneca the younger in the middle of the last Millennium by Racine and many times over since including relatively recently by Sarah Kane it's always been a tale of forbidden love originally the princess falling in love with her stepson but in this new version the young man is already in his 40s and he's the son of a former lover so not a stepson and certainly not a young man being taken advantage of The Forbidden Love here is on the face of it that of someone whose passionate feelings lead her into infidelity simple adultery although not that simple as it turns out I guess most of us can understand the way love or lust can overtake reason our protagonist called not Federer but Helen is a shadow cabinet minister you could say that her Forbidden love is not so much for someone other than her husband but her love of herself because this is a play dominated by an examination of a certain kind of liberal middle-class people who appear to have no moral code beyond what they feel we first meet to family bickering over breakfast a teenage son is uncontrolled in his language and subject matter in front of and indeed towards his parents older daughter who's just visiting is not much less restrained the affable father jokes with them about sex uh it seems to be a family without boundaries well so what the liberal principles of treating the children as equals as quasi-grown-ups may be admirable but in this case the children do seem to have become self-centered and lacking in respect Helen their mother leads by example and this is most brought home by the way they speak over one another barely listening again your own opinions about bringing up children they mean that you find this scene appalling or laugh out loud funny or both and we also see or a meant to see an English for which we first world or or imperialists even indifference to other cultures for example when Helen spent time earlier in her life in Morocco she didn't bother to learn the language and she hasn't bothered to find out where her black best friend was born then sophiana arrives he reminds Helen of his father her past Moroccan lover and he makes clear he reciprocates the feelings that she has for him it's not just that he's like his father physically he too is a political activist and that reminds her even more of how she has traded physical excitement for a boring marriage and given up the thrill of activism for the compromise of Party politics but I don't need to tell you how often an older person has an affair to try to recapture their lost youth despite the changes to the plot and the modern setting this is still a Greek tragedy in its structure so I won't go any further with the story except to say Simon Stone has retained those ancient ideas that people who misbehave get punished and revenge moves through the generations so there are many twists and it does all end badly in fact the ending is very dramatic almost melodramatic it's a well-told story with much comedy and many great sets scenes one in particular takes place in a restaurant where the family and close friends are gathered for Helen's 60th birthday Revolution follows Revelation in a scene that wouldn't go missing a farce with glasses smashing home truth spewing out and hell and all the while lamenting loudly about the distraction from her celebration the acting is marvelous Janet mcteer is so on point as this totally self-absorbed politician she talks at speed with passion and intensity and expresses her feeling so naturally that you forget she's acting I felt we were already witnessing one of the acting performances of the year with a scripter match Paul Shahidi as her husband Huga is terrific too in the role of this put upon husband and father who manages to keep afloat with jokes and diplomacy he's charming and likable but also exudes insignificance you can see why he appealed to the dominating Helen but also why she was ready to be unfaithful to sofiane played by the handsome charismatic Assad ruap all the cast impressed but a special word for Akia Henry as Helen's friend and fellow Shadow Cabinet member omolara she portrays an easy going person who seems to take Helen's ignorance of her background and her mockery of her religion with good humor but you sense an iron core that emanates from her moral grounding something Helen lacks and she has the kind of painted smile that conceals an objective calculating mind so what didn't I like well the design all the action takes place within a glass box which revolves now this was an interesting coincidence because only the night before I saw Federer I saw the Lehman Trilogy which also features a revolving glass box but whereas the latter worked this didn't the effect is perhaps of making us feel like the Greek or Roman gods who would look down on humans and their folly or perhaps it could suggest the way in which the characters are trapped in this case in the cycle of betrayal and revenge the many uprights may have been intended to reinforce the idea of the characters being in a prison but they too often obscured the faces of the actors and that was a shame not to be able to see the agonies their characters were going through but the biggest problem caused by the design is that every change of scene took forever sometimes the scene change was longer than the following scene I imagine this was because when the action takes place simply on the stage floor in most Productions scenery can be rolled on and off easily but when you're dealing with a raised glass box with awkward access and egress everything takes much longer the extended blackouts would frankly been intolerable but for Stefan Gregory's sound which played while we waited and which was hypnotic now designer Chloe langford's Talent is beyond question the sets within the Box did actually look fantastic it's just that the Box itself didn't work I don't want to lay all the blame on at her door because it could well be that she was simply doing what director Simon Stone wanted uh the last production by him that I saw was yerma at the Young Vic great production but that too took place behind glass walls so maybe it's his thing anyway a wonderful script first class acting both worthy of a five-star production let down only by the design even so I give fedra at the National Theater four stars I hope you enjoyed this review and please like comment and best of all
